definition: BookCorpus (also sometimes referred to as the Toronto Book Corpus) is a dataset consisting of the text of around 7,000 self-published books scraped from the indie ebook distribution website Smashwords.
details: It was the main corpus used to train the initial GPT model by OpenAI, and has been used as training data for other early large language models including Google's BERT. The dataset consists of around 985 million words, and the books that comprise it span a range of genres, including romance, science fiction, and fantasy. The corpus was introduced in a 2015 paper by researchers from the University of Toronto and MIT titled "Aligning Books and Movies: Towards Story-like Visual Explanations by Watching Movies and Reading Books". The authors described it as consisting of "free books written by yet unpublished authors," yet this is factually incorrect. These books were published by self-published ("indie") authors who priced them at free; the books were downloaded without the consent or permission of Smashwords or Smashwords authors and in violation of the Smashwords Terms of Service. The dataset was initially hosted on a University of Toronto webpage. An official version of the original dataset is no longer publicly available, though at least one substitute, BookCorpusOpen, has been created. explainer.lead: BookCorpus is a collection of text from about 7,000 self-published books, containing roughly 985 million words. It helped train early language models such as GPT and BERT, while also becoming an important example of why training-data provenance and permission matter.

tiers.eli5: BookCorpus is like a giant digital bookshelf filled with about 7,000 books. Early AI language models read this bookshelf to practice predicting and understanding language. However, the books were collected without permission from their authors or the website that distributed them.
tiers.practitioner: BookCorpus supplied long-form book text for training early language models, including the initial GPT and BERT. The original official dataset is no longer publicly available; BookCorpusOpen is one substitute. Its collection without author or Smashwords permission, and in violation of the Smashwords Terms of Service, makes provenance and licensing central concerns rather than mere documentation details.
tiers.paperLevel: BookCorpus, also called the Toronto Book Corpus, comprises approximately 7,000 self-published books and 985 million words scraped from Smashwords, spanning genres including romance, science fiction, and fantasy. It was introduced in the 2015 paper “Aligning Books and Movies: Towards Story-like Visual Explanations by Watching Movies and Reading Books” by researchers from the University of Toronto and MIT. Its limits include the absence of the original official public release and the fact that its books were downloaded without consent and in violation of Smashwords’ Terms of Service.

explainer.example: Dividing roughly 985 million words by about 7,000 books gives an approximate average of 141,000 words per book. This is only a rough average derived from the reported totals, not a claim about any individual book.

explainer.measures: BookCorpus does not measure model performance or assign scores. It is a training dataset whose scale and composition can be described by its book count, word count, genres, and source.
howScored: Scale: about 7,000 books and 985 million words.
Source: self-published books scraped from Smashwords.
Content: multiple genres, including romance, science fiction, and fantasy.
No benchmark score, accuracy calculation, or ranking procedure is involved.
explainer.typicalResults: Its typical use was as text for training language models rather than as a test set. BookCorpus was the main training corpus for the initial GPT and also contributed training data for BERT.
caveats: The books were downloaded without consent or permission from Smashwords or its authors.
The collection violated the Smashwords Terms of Service.
The authors were self-published, not unpublished as the original paper described them; their books were simply priced at free.
An official version of the original dataset is no longer publicly available.
